records.task: On the Ada Lovelace Wikipedia article (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ada_Lovelace) in my browser, read the section about her work and sum it up in three sentences, from what the page says.
records.answer: Ada Lovelace translated an article on Charles Babbage's Analytical Engine and added extensive notes that described how the machine could be programmed to solve complex problems. These notes included an algorithm for calculating Bernoulli numbers, often cited as the first published computer program, though historians debate whether she or Babbage was the primary author. Beyond this specific calculation, Lovelace recognized that the engine could manipulate any symbols represented by numbers, such as musical notes, and famously argued that the machine could only follow instructions rather than originate new ideas.

records.task: On the Ada Lovelace Wikipedia article (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ada_Lovelace) in my browser, read the section about her work and sum it up in three sentences, from what the page says.
records.answer: Ada Lovelace translated Luigi Menabrea's French transcription of Charles Babbage's lecture on the Analytical Engine into English and augmented it with seven extensive notes (A-G) that were about three times longer than the original translation. Her Note G described in complete detail a method for calculating Bernoulli numbers using the Analytical Engine, which is often called the first published computer program, though there is controversy over whether she or Babbage deserved primary credit for the algorithm. Lovelace's most significant contribution was her insight that the Analytical Engine could manipulate symbols beyond mere numbers—such as musical notes or letters—anticipating the concept of general-purpose computation a century before it was realized.

records.task: On the Ada Lovelace Wikipedia article (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ada_Lovelace) in my browser, read the section about her work and sum it up in three sentences, from what the page says.
records.answer: Ada Lovelace translated Luigi Menabrea's French paper on Babbage's Analytical Engine and added extensive Notes A-G, with Note G containing what is often called the first published computer program—an algorithm for calculating Bernoulli numbers. She recognized that the Analytical Engine could manipulate symbols beyond just numbers, anticipating modern general-purpose computing by noting it could compose music or handle any process expressible through logical operations. Lovelace also distinguished between the mechanical aspects of computing devices and their logical structure, and articulated what became known as "Lady Lovelace's Objection" to artificial intelligence, stating that the engine could only perform tasks it was explicitly programmed to do and could not originate anything on its own.
